claimText: The trinitarian wording known as the Johannine Comma in 1 John 5:7 ('in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one') is a later textual addition, not part of the original text of 1 John 5:7-8.

sourcesChecked.source: Daniel B. Wallace, 'The Textual Problem in 1 John 5:7-8' (bible.org)
NET Bible, 1 John 5:7-8 (quoted in the bible.org article)
sourcesChecked.edition: NET Bible
sourcesChecked.locator: 1 John 5:7-8: 'For there are three that testify, the Spirit and the water and the blood, and these three are in agreement.'

sourcesChecked.source: Bible Hub Q&A, 'Why is 1 John 5:7 absent in some early Greek manuscripts?' (search result read)
sourcesChecked.locator: http://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_1_John_5_7_missing_in_some_texts.htm — Vaticanus (B, 4th c.) and Sinaiticus (א, 4th c.) lack the Comma; NA28 and UBS5 place it in the apparatus, not the main text

evidenceFound: Wallace (bible.org): 'This longer reading is found only in eight late manuscripts, four of which have the words in a marginal note. Most of these manuscripts (2318, 221, and [with minor variations] 61, 88, 429, 629, 636, and 918) originate from the 16th century; the earliest manuscript, codex 221 (10th century), includes the reading in a marginal note which was added sometime after the original composition. Thus, there is no sure evidence of this reading in any Greek manuscript until the 1500s.' Further: 'the reading appears in no Greek witness of any kind (either manuscript, patristic, or Greek translation of some other version) until AD 1215 (in a Greek translation of the Acts of the Lateran Council, a work originally written in Latin).' 'The reading seems to have arisen in a fourth century Latin homily.' It 'made its way into the third edition of Erasmus' Greek NT (1522) because of pressure from the Catholic Church' after codex 61 (written c. 1520) was produced. Corroborated by Bible Hub: the two oldest complete Greek codices, Vaticanus (4th c.) and Sinaiticus (4th c.), lack the Comma, and critical editions (Nestle-Aland 28, UBS 5) place it in the apparatus. This is new checked manuscript evidence beyond Phase 2, which had only compared ESV and KJV renderings; it upgrades Phase 2 record ver-1john-5-7-comma-001 (not-verified) to verified.
limitations: Verification rests on the documentary survey in the sources read (Wallace's summary of the manuscript evidence, citing Metzger, Textual Commentary, 2nd ed., 647-49), not on a manuscript-by-manuscript inspection by this checker. The minority position (Cyprian/Priscillian allusions, homoeoteleuton omission argument) is noted in the Bible Hub source but does not overturn the documentary evidence; a reader wanting the full debate should consult Metzger directly.

claimText: Origen argues that Wisdom, understood as the beginning of the ways of God, is also to be understood as the Word of God, because she discloses the mysteries of divine wisdom to creation. John, he says, defines God as the Word with more sublimity: 'And God was the Word, and this was in the beginning with God.' Whoever assigns a beginning to the Word or Wisdom, Origen warns, is guilty of impiety against the unbegotten Father, since that would deny the Father had always been Father.

claimText: Athanasius quotes the Thalia of Arius to exhibit the Arian doctrine: God was not always Father but became Father; the Son was not always, but was made out of nothing, 'once was not', and had an origin of creation like other creatures; God made him Word and Wisdom and Son in order to form us by means of him. In §6 Athanasius adds that Arius held the Word to be 'not the very God' but God only in name, by participation of grace, 'alien and unlike in all things to the Father's essence'.

evidenceFound: Athanasius, Discourse I, ch. 2, heading: 'Extracts from the Thalia of Arius. Arius maintains that God became a Father, and the Son was not always; the Son out of nothing; once He was not; He was not before his generation; He was created; named Wisdom and Word after God's attributes; made that He might make us'; section 5: '"God was not always a Father"; but "once God was alone, and not yet a Father, but afterwards He became a Father." "The Son was not always"; for, whereas all things were made out of nothing... so the Word of God Himself was "made out of nothing," and "once He was not," and "He was not before His origination"... "thereupon He made a certain one, and named Him Word and Wisdom and Son, that He might form us by means of Him"'; section 6: '"the Word is not the very God"; though He is called God, yet He is not very God, but by participation of grace, He, as others, is God only in name... the Word [is] alien and unlike in all things to the Father's essence'. Athanasius introduces the material as 'the commencement of Arius's Thalia... runs thus' - the Thalia survives only as quoted by Athanasius, a hostile witness.

claimText: Athanasius opens Discourse IV by proving the substantiality of the Word from Scripture: the Word is God from God because John says 'the Word was God', and Paul says Christ is 'God over all' (Romans 9:5). claimText: Hilary recounts his own conversion through reading John 1:1-14: his soul learned from the Gospel that the Word was with God and was God, that the Word became flesh, and that his glory was seen as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. From this he learned that the Creator is 'God of God': faith is not dispersed among many deities, nor is a difference of nature attributed to this God of God. In §10 he quotes the whole of John 1:1-14, and in §13 he argues that the Word's 'was' has no limit of time and no commencement: 'the uncreated Word was in the beginning.'

claimText: Gregory traces how the Spirit was 'declared by Jesus' by little and little: 'I will ask the Father, He says, and He will send you another Comforter, even the spirit of Truth' (John 14:16). Jesus said this, Gregory explains, 'that He might not seem to be a rival God, or to make His discourses to them by another authority.' The Spirit then came gradually to dwell in the disciples, 'measuring Himself out to them according to their capacity to receive Him'. In §3 Gregory had already called the Spirit 'the Other Comforter' and 'the True Light which lighteneth every man coming into the world', one Light with Father and Son.

claimText: Answering the dilemma that the Spirit must be either Unbegotten or Begotten, Gregory appeals to the Saviour's own word: 'The Holy Ghost, which proceedeth from the Father' (John 15:26). Procession is the Spirit's distinctive mode: because he proceeds from the Father he is no creature; because he is not begotten he is no Son; and because he stands between the Unbegotten and the Begotten, he is God. 'What then is Procession?' Gregory asks, and answers that it is as unexplainable as the Father's unbegottenness and the Son's generation.

sourcesChecked.locator: https://etheses.durham.ac.uk/id/eprint/5522/1/5522_2961-vol1.PDF - defends genuine Athanasian authorship (read via web search results)

evidenceFound: New Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Athanasius, St. Dogmatic [Writings]': 'The discourses were written, in all probability, during his third exile (c. 358). A fourth Discourse, added in the Benedictine and Migne editions, is now considered as definitely spurious.' Catholic Culture (Quasten): 'A number of manuscripts add a fourth Discourse, but whereas the first three form a homogeneous work, the forth differs in address, content, and style. In fact, it is not written against the Arians at all but against the Marcellians'; 'The first three discourses form a single continuous work by Athanasius; the fourth was added later by an unknown author.' Vinzent (Brill, 1996) argues Contra Arianos IV was written c. 340 as a Nicene critique of Marcellus, with Apollinaris of Laodicea as a possible author. Walbrodt (Durham MA thesis, 1993) defends genuine Athanasian authorship. The dispute is therefore real and unresolved; the research file's work-level note flags it, but the three Discourse IV interpretation records do not.
limitations: Scholarship is divided: the New Catholic Encyclopedia and Quasten treat Discourse IV as spurious/added by an unknown author, while Walbrodt (1993) argues it is genuinely Athanasian. The dispute itself is verified; no side is endorsed here. The three Discourse IV interpretation records in this set are therefore partially-verified, not verified.

sourcesChecked.source: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, Vol. VI: The Middle Ages, A.D. 1294-1517, section 18, 'The Council of Ferrara-Florence, 1438-1445'
sourcesChecked.edition: Schaff, History of the Christian Church, Vol. VI (CCEL)
sourcesChecked.locator: https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/hcc6/hcc6.iii.iii.vii.html - 'The articles were signed July 5 by 115 Latins and 33 Greeks, of whom 18 were metropolitans. Archbishop Mark of Ephesus was the only one of the Orientals who refused to sign.'; 'On July 6, 1439, the articles were publicly read in the cathedral of Florence, the Greek text by Bessarion, and the Latin by Cesarini.'

evidenceFound: The articles of union were incorporated in a decree beginning Laetentur coeli et exultat terra. The articles were signed July 5 by 115 Latins and 33 Greeks. Archbishop Mark of Ephesus was the only one of the Orientals who refused to sign. On July 6, 1439, the articles were publicly read in the cathedral of Florence.
limitations: The decree states that 'texts were produced from divine scriptures' in the debate, but the checked text names no specific biblical passage by reference, so no passage is listed; do not pad. The union was rejected in the East: the patriarchs of Jerusalem, Antioch, and Alexandria issued a letter from Jerusalem in 1443 denouncing the council of Florence. The decree's definition is the Latin West's position, with the Eastern disagreement noted.

claimText: The Racovian Catechism (1605) is a publication, exact date 1605: first published in the Polish language at Rakow in 1605 (Latin version 1609). It argues that Matthew 28:19, 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, and 1 John 5:7 prove only the existence and association of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in divine things, not three persons in one essence. It is linked to passages matt-28-19, 1cor-12-4, and 1john-5-7; authorIds is empty because authorship is collective.

sourcesChecked.source: The Racovian Catechism, trans. Thomas Rees
sourcesChecked.edition: Rees translation (London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680; archive.org
sourcesChecked.locator: Section III, ch. 1, pp. 54-57, and Historical Introduction, pp. lxxvii-lxxviii; https://archive.org/stream/racoviancatechi00reesgoog/racoviancatechi00reesgoog_djvu.txt

evidenceFound: Section III, Chapter 1: 'I answer generally in respect to them, that they only prove the existence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and that they are associated in divine things... It is evident, nevertheless, that these testimonies do not prove the matter in dispute; namely, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are three persons in the one essence of God.' The three testimonies named together are Matthew 28:19, 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, and 1 John 5:7. Rees's Historical Introduction: 'the work, as modelled and completed by these eminent persons, was first published in the Polish language in duodecimo, in 1605.'
limitations: Dissenting milestone. Authorship is collective (Smalcius, Moskorzowski, Volkel; Socinus died 1604, before drafting), so authorIds is empty here; the associated author is recorded on the work record. Passages matt-28-19, 1cor-12-4, and 1john-5-7 all exist in the inventory.

claimText: The readings in the Racovian Catechism are attributed to the Socinian tradition associated with Faustus Socinus, who died in 1604 before the Catechism was drafted; the Catechism was completed by Valentinus Smalcius, Hieronim Moskorzowski, and Johannes Volkel, and first published in Polish in 1605.

sourcesChecked.source: The Racovian Catechism, trans. Thomas Rees
sourcesChecked.edition: Rees translation (London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680; archive.org

evidenceFound: Rees's Historical Introduction: 'Sandius states that the task of revising or reforming the first Racovian Catechism was assigned to Faustus Socinus and Peter Statorius junior... They were, however, both prevented by the hand of death from completing their undertaking; and it was in consequence transferred to Valentine Smalcius and Jerome Moscorovius, with whom it would appear that Volkelius also was associated. The work, as modelled and completed by these eminent persons, was first published in the Polish language in duodecimo, in 1605.' The Introduction also states that some text may have been prepared by Socinus, and that his fragments 'can hardly be deemed entitled to this distinction... the entire form is different... imperfect sketches'.
limitations: PARTIALLY VERIFIED: the research files DO flag the disputed authorship correctly in the notes - the four Socinus interpretations each state that the reading is the Catechism's / Socinian tradition, not Socinus as sole author, and the milestone racovian-catechism-1605 correctly has empty authorIds with a collective-authorship note. BUT the structured data still attributes the material to Socinus alone: works.json lists authorIds [faustus-socrinus] for racovian-catechism (with disputedAuthorship: true and an explanatory note), and all four interpretations in this pass carry authorId faustus-socrinus. Read without the notes, the structured attribution names Socinus as the author of a work drafted after his death. The attribution is therefore only partially verified at the data level; the structured authorIds should be corrected or the notes made structurally explicit before publication. Socinus's personal contribution to the text is likely but not individually established; the Catechism is a collective work of the Polish Brethren.
notes: Dev 1 second-pass verification (Phase 4); independent QA verification per RESEARCH-STANDARDS §9.2 still required. Not publishable without independent verification and editorial approval.
